nameStory: This plant earned its name 'hairy lespedeza' from the soft, fuzzy hairs that cover its stems and leaves - run your fingers along them and you'll feel the velvety texture immediately. The genus name Lespedeza honors Vicente Manuel de Céspedes, an 18th-century Spanish governor of East Florida who supported botanical exploration. Its alternate name 'hairy bush clover' reflects both its fuzzy appearance and its membership in the legume family, where it's related to true clovers.
description: Hairy lespedeza is a native wildflower that looks like a small, fuzzy shrub growing up to three feet tall. This perennial belongs to the legume family (the same group as beans and peas) and produces clusters of tiny white flowers in summer. The entire plant has a soft, velvety feel due to fine hairs covering the stems and leaves. It's a tough prairie plant that thrives in average to dry soils and supports many butterfly and moth species.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms an upright, bushy clump reaching up to three feet tall with multiple branching stems that feel distinctly soft and fuzzy to the touch

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Three-part leaves (like clover) covered in fine, soft hairs that give them a velvety, grayish-green appearance - stroke them gently to feel the fuzziness

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny white flowers clustered along the stems in summer, each bloom less than half an inch long and typical pea-family shape with a banner petal

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Densely covered in soft, fine hairs that make the entire stem feel like velvet - this hairiness is visible as a grayish fuzz in good light

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small, flattened pods typical of legumes, each containing one or two seeds and persisting into fall

habitat: Look for hairy lespedeza in dry, open areas like prairies, old fields, roadsides, and woodland edges throughout New England. It thrives in well-drained, average to poor soils and full sun to partial shade. You'll often find it growing alongside other native prairie plants and grasses in restored grasslands or natural openings.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as fuzzy, three-part leaves on soft-haired stems. The velvety texture of young foliage is especially pronounced in spring.
seasonality.summer: Small white flowers appear in clusters along the stems from mid to late summer. This is prime identification time when both the hairy foliage and characteristic pea-family flowers are visible.
seasonality.fall: Flowers give way to small seed pods while the fuzzy leaves may turn yellowish before dying back. Seeds ripen and disperse in early fall.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to the ground as a perennial, leaving dried stems and seed pods that may persist. The root system remains alive underground.

funFact: Hairy lespedeza is like a butterfly nursery buffet - it serves as a host plant for the caterpillars of at least eight different moth and butterfly species, including the beautiful cloudless sulphur butterfly and the striking bella moth, making it one of the most valuable native plants for supporting Lepidoptera in New England!
confusionNotes: The fuzzy, three-part leaves distinguish it from most other plants, but it can be confused with other bush clovers in the same genus. Remember: if it feels soft and velvety all over with white flowers, you've found hairy lespedeza - the 'velvet touch' is your best clue.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'bush clover,' this plant isn't a true clover (Trifolium) but rather a member of the broader legume family. Like true clovers, it can fix nitrogen in the soil through root bacteria, making it valuable for soil improvement in restoration projects.
compareHints: Among New England's bush clovers, hairy lespedeza stands out for its distinctly fuzzy, velvety texture covering the entire plant. Round-headed bush clover has dense, globe-shaped flower clusters rather than the scattered small clusters of hairy lespedeza. Violet bush clover produces purple flowers instead of white ones, making the color difference an easy distinguishing feature.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Round-headed bush clover stands out from its Lespedeza relatives by its distinctly round, compact flower heads - most other bush clovers have loose, elongated flower clusters or flowers scattered along the stems.
Among its bush clover relatives, violet bush clover stands out with its smooth (not hairy) stems and leaves, and its loose flower arrangement rather than dense round clusters.
Among New England's bush clovers, Chinese bushclover stands out for its silvery, densely hairy appearance and aggressive colonial growth habit.
Among New England's bush clovers, slender bush clover stands out for its delicate, wispy appearance with thin stems and small flower clusters.

Among its bush-clover relatives, tall bush-clover stands out with its reliably erect stems - round-headed bush clover has similar upright growth but denser, more rounded flower clusters, while violet bush clover and trailing lespedeza have more sprawling or leaning growth habits.
Among the many Lespedeza species, shrub lespedeza is unique in New England for its tall, shrubby growth habit - most other bush clovers in our region are low-growing or trailing plants.
Unlike its upright relatives like round-headed bush clover or hairy lespedeza that can reach several feet tall, trailing lespedeza never gets off the ground.
Among its bush clover relatives, narrow-leaved bush clover stands out for its distinctly slender leaflets and preference for wet soils.
Among the bush clovers in New England, violet bush clover stands out for its distinctly purple-violet flowers - most of its relatives have white, cream, or very pale pink blooms.
Among the lespedezas, Thunberg's is unique for its dramatic weeping form - most other bush clovers in New England grow upright or spreading but not with these long, graceful drooping branches.
While most of its lespedeza relatives like round-headed bush clover and violet bush clover grow upright in bushy clumps, creeping lespedeza is the ground-hugger of the family.
Downy lespedeza stands out from other bush clovers in New England primarily by its extremely fuzzy, silvery appearance.
